n: The three friends give up because Job insists he is innocent. The narrator steps back in, in prose, to introduce a new speaker.
A younger man, Elihu, has been listening. He burns with anger at Job for defending himself more than defending God. Elihu is not mentioned before or after his speeches (chapters 32–37).

f.g: The name means “He is my God.”
Buz was a relative of Abraham.

n: He is also angry with the three friends: they condemned Job but had no real answer to his arguments.

f.w: had found no answer, and yet had condemned Job

n: Out of respect for age, Elihu waited until the older men were finished.

f.w: because they were elder than he

n: When he saw the three had nothing more to say, his anger flared.

f.w: no answer in the mouth of these three men
f.g: Their silence shows they have lost the debate.

n: Elihu begins (in poetry) by explaining that he is young and hesitated to speak in front of older men.
He thought age and years of experience should teach wisdom.

f.g: Those with many days — the elderly — should speak first.

n: But Elihu realizes that real understanding comes from the spirit God gives a person, not merely from age.

f.w: there is a spirit in man
the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding

n: Being important or old does not guarantee being wise or knowing what is right.
So Elihu asks them to listen to him; he too will share what he knows.
He waited patiently and listened to all their arguments as they searched for words.

f.w: I gave ear to your reasons
f.g: I listened carefully to your arguments.

n: He paid close attention, but not one of them proved Job wrong or answered his words.

f.w: none of you that convinced Job

n: Don’t claim you’ve found wisdom by saying, “Only God can defeat him, not us.” Elihu thinks a human answer is possible.

f.w: God thrusteth him down, not man
f.g: The friends might excuse their failure by leaving Job to God.

n: Job hasn’t argued with Elihu directly, so Elihu won’t answer with the friends’ tired arguments.

f.w: neither will I answer him with your speeches

n: Elihu describes the friends as stunned and silent, with nothing left to say.
He waited, but they just stood there and said nothing more.
So he decides to give his part of the answer.

f.g: Contribute my share to the debate.

n: He is bursting with words; the spirit inside him presses him to speak.
Like new wine in sealed wineskins, he feels ready to burst.

f.g: New wineskins; fermenting wine would make them swell.

n: Speaking will bring him relief.
Elihu promises to be impartial — no favoritism and no flattery toward anyone.
He doesn’t know how to flatter; if he did, his Maker would soon carry him away. Readers debate whether Elihu’s confidence is wisdom or youthful overconfidence.

f.g: Empty honorifics used to win favor.

f.w: my maker would soon take me away
